text: You've got variables, types, strings, and collections. Now it's time to make code actually react to data: if, elif, and else for branching, for and while loops for repeating, and break and continue for controlling exactly how a loop flows — all applied to validating a real batch of order records.

A conditional runs different code depending on whether an expression is True or False. Python checks each condition top to bottom and runs the first branch that's True, then skips the rest. elif and else are optional, but else is your catch-all — exactly the branch that catches an order with a negative quantity.

A for loop runs its body once per item in a collection — this is how you'll process every row of real data for the rest of this course. Check a condition, and continue past a bad row — skipping whatever comes after it for that row — otherwise process it normally. That check-then-continue pattern is the backbone of real-world data validation.

A while loop keeps running as long as its condition stays True — the right tool when you don't know in advance how many times you'll repeat, like retrying a failed connection. Here, attempts stays under three until connected becomes True. Forgetting to change the condition inside the loop is the classic way to write an infinite loop.

break stops a loop immediately, regardless of its condition. Once you've found the order you're looking for, there's no reason to keep checking the rest of the list — break exits right away instead of wastefully looping through everything that's left.

That wraps up Chapter 1 — you can now store, clean, and branch on real data. But the validation logic you just wrote was inline, copy-pasted into a loop. Chapter 2 starts with writing functions — turning that exact logic into a reusable, named, testable piece of code you call from anywhere.
